Horror
hŏr´ẽr
n. (a shuddering dread; in Genesis the darkness that fell on Abram before the covenant was cut)
Latin horror, a bristling, a shuddering, from horrere, to bristle with fear. Hebrew eymah, terror; pallatsuth, shuddering; zilaphah, the burning horror of indignation.

Biblical Definition

Before God made the covenant with Abram, He put him out of the way: “when the sun was going down, a deep sleep fell upon Abram; and, lo, an horror of great darkness fell upon him” (Gen 15:12). David knows it in flight: “Fearfulness and trembling are come upon me, and horror hath overwhelmed me” (Psa 55:5). Psalm 119 gives it a righteous object: “Horror hath taken hold upon me because of the wicked that forsake thy law” (Psa 119:53). Ezekiel gives it to a people under judgment: “horror shall cover them; and shame shall be upon all faces” (Eze 7:18).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines horror as a shaking, shivering or shuddering, as in the cold fit which precedes a fever; and a powerful excitement of fear and dread, or terror mingled with detestation.

expand to see more

HORROR, n. A shaking, shivering or shuddering, as in the cold fit which precedes a fever.

HORROR, n. An excessive degree of fear, or a painful emotion which makes a person tremble; terror; a shuddering with fear.

HORROR, n. Terror or dread mingled with detestation; that which excites horror.

Key Scripture

Gen 15:12 — "And when the sun was going down, a deep sleep fell upon Abram; and, lo, an horror of great darkness fell upon him."

Psa 55:5 — "Fearfulness and trembling are come upon me, and horror hath overwhelmed me."

Psa 119:53 — "Horror hath taken hold upon me because of the wicked that forsake thy law."

Eze 7:18 — "They shall also gird themselves with sackcloth, and horror shall cover them; and shame shall be upon all faces, and baldness upon all their heads."

Modern Corruption

Abram was put to sleep in horror and darkness while God alone passed between the pieces, which is why the covenant cannot fail.

expand to see more

Genesis 15 is the foundation of the doctrine of the unconditional covenant. The animals are divided and the pieces laid opposite each other in the ordinary form of a covenant-cutting, in which both parties walk the aisle and invoke on themselves the fate of the beasts if they break faith. Abram never walks it. A horror of great darkness falls on him, he sleeps, and a smoking furnace and a burning lamp pass between the pieces alone. God binds Himself on both sides. Every promise in that covenant therefore rests on the faithfulness of one party, which is why Hebrews 6 calls it two immutable things in which it is impossible for God to lie.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that horror is not always a symptom to be relieved. Psalm 119:53 attaches it to a righteous cause — horror hath taken hold upon me because of the wicked that forsake thy law — and the psalmist offers it as evidence of love for God, not as a disorder. Scripture has room for a settled dread at what sin is and where it goes. The therapeutic instinct that treats every strong negative feeling as pathology cannot make sense of that verse, and a church that has lost the capacity for it will not be able to make sense of Ezekiel 7 either.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew eymah (H367), terror, dread; pallatsuth (H6427), shuddering, horror; zilaphah (H2152), burning indignation.

Hebrew eymah (H367) — terror, dread; Genesis 15:12, Exodus 15:16, Job 9:34.

Hebrew pallatsuth (H6427) — shuddering, horror; Psalm 55:5, Isaiah 21:4, Ezekiel 7:18.

Hebrew zilaphah (H2152) — burning horror, indignation; Psalm 11:6, 119:53.

Hebrew berith (H1285) — covenant; Genesis 15:18, 17:7.

Usage

"“An horror of great darkness fell upon him” — Abram while God passed alone."

"“Horror hath overwhelmed me” — David in flight."

"“Horror hath taken hold upon me because of the wicked” — horror with a righteous cause."
